tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of the ICM organization's 370-person personnel situation from the supplied data (Table 1: seven position levels with headcounts, salaries, recruitment times/costs, training costs, all in units of sigma, the company's median income), describing the model and all assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: The supplied data is aggregate (seven levels, no individual roster), so the network is built as a layered star graph that is the only structure the data can support: each employee reports to exactly one supervisor in the level above (uniformly at random), and a single CEO sits above the ten senior managers. This is the standard org-chart (arborescence) representation of a hierarchical firm; individual assignment of the 370 named seats is impossible from aggregate counts, and any denser 'friendship' or 'influence' structure would be fabricated, so the bold assumption is that the reporting layer IS the Human Capital network, with other layers (task 6) attached later. The graph has 371 nodes and 370 edges, average degree 1.995, max degree 10 (a junior manager supervising up to ten subordinates), median degree 1, and depth 7 (CEO to administrative clerk). All monetary quantities are carried in sigma per the dataset definition; sigma itself is never needed in absolute dollars. The data were cleaned before modelling: the sigma symbol arrived as a mojibake byte pair (0xA6 0xD2) in 21 cells, was decoded as latin-1 and replaced; the Experienced-employee average-salary cell was a bare symbol with its coefficient lost in transmission and was imputed to 1.0 sigma, the unique value that makes the weighted median of all 370 salaries equal sigma as the dataset definition requires (the 110 experienced-employee seats straddle the 185th-186th rank of the 370, so their level average IS the company median); a trailing blank line was dropped; headcounts sum exactly to 370.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes V = {CEO} union level seats (|V| = 371); directed edges E = {(u,v): v supervises u}, |E| = 370, out-degree 1 for every non-CEO node. Level populations N = (10, 20, 25, 25, 110, 150, 30) for (senior mgr, junior mgr, exp. supervisor, inex. supervisor, exp. employee, inex. employee, clerk); salaries in sigma s = (8, 4, 2, 1.5, 1.0, 0.9, 0.9); recruitment lead times in months t = (7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 1, 2); recruitment costs in sigma c = (1.2, 0.7, 0.6, 0.6, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3); training costs in sigma/yr tr = (0.5, 0.6, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.05). Betweenness on the tree: the unique shortest path between two nodes passes through exactly the path nodes, so b(v) = (subtree size of v - 1) x (371 - subtree size of v), computed exactly for all 371 nodes. Statistics: avg degree 1.995, max degree 10, median degree 1, longest path 7 hops; middle layer (junior mgrs + both supervisor classes, 102 seats) holds 76.7% of the top-30 betweenness nodes and averages 3.34x the company mean betweenness (4621 vs 1383 in path-pair units).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The middle management layer is the network's structural bottleneck: nearly three quarters of the most central nodes are middle managers, so a departure there removes more of the firm's connective tissue per person than a departure at any other level. This is the network-theoretic expression of problem issue 4 (middle managers 'stuck', critical, high turnover) and it predicts that middle-layer churn is disproportionately damaging to information flow and coordination, not just to raw headcount. Limitations: the uniform random assignment of subordinates to supervisors is a symmetry assumption forced by the aggregate data — real org charts have preferred attachment (star vs chain variation); the model measures structural position, not individual talent; and betweenness on a tree overstates the betweenness of any single edge in a real firm with informal lateral links (which task 6 adds). Bias: the model is blind to quality differences within a level (issue 8's 'marginal employees stay'), so its headcount is a capacity count, not a capability count.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and incorporate the dynamic processes within the Human Capital network: (1) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction) and (2) direct and indirect effects on organizational productivity.
tasks.task_analysis: Churn is modelled as a monthly discrete-time stochastic process at level granularity (individual resolution is impossible without a roster). The dynamics have four coupled components. (a) Independent baseline hazard: each level has a monthly quit probability p0(level) = 1 - exp(-r(level)/12), with annual rates pinned to the two data anchors in the problem — the company-wide weighted rate is 18% (CEO quote, issue 7) and the middle tiers (102 of 370 seats) churn at twice the rest (issue 4), giving r_mid = 0.2718 and r_rest = 0.1359 exactly. (b) Peer contagion [E1]: an expert exchange confirmed that quits cluster within work groups and that a departed close colleague raises a colleague's quit hazard by roughly 10-50% in relative terms over the following months, while the bulk of separations remain independent. The model adds a hazard multiplier min(3.0, 1 + 0.30 x per-team effective recent departures), where effective recent departures decay with a 3-month half-life and are spread over the level's ~10-person teams; a global multiplier beta in [0,2] scales the whole contagion term (beta=0 is the independent baseline the expert called a reasonable first-order approximation; beta=1 is the base case). (c) Absorbed workload and ramp-up [E2]: a second expert exchange established that remaining teammates absorb part of a departed person's work rather than the seat simply idling; the model charges 40% of each vacant seat as deferred backlog (the team absorbs 60%), a new hire works at 50% capacity during the level's Table-1 recruitment lead time, and a decaying load-shock (3-month half-life) tracks the overtime strain. (d) Promotion pipeline: internal promotion fills departures from the level below at rates f = (0.5, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3) subject to a qualified-candidate constraint (half of the below-level pool meets the experience requirement of issue 6); the vacated lower seat becomes an ordinary vacancy. External recruiting runs under the issue-5 capacity constraint: about 33 active searches at once (9% of 370), covering 2/3 of vacancies, each completing after its level's median time-to-recruit. Productivity: an employee produces sigma x salary coefficient per year; the firm's output is the sum over filled seats, so lost output is the vacancy backlog plus the new-hire ramp, valued at each level's salary (an unfilled senior seat costs 8x an unfilled clerk seat per month).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State at month m: pop_i(m) filled seats, vac_i(m) vacancies, pending_i(m) in-flight searches, recent_i(m) = {age of recent departures}, load_i(m) absorbed load. Transitions (per level i, sublevel set {i}): q_i ~ Binomial(pop_i, p_i) with p_i = min(0.5, p0_i x min(3, 1 + 0.30 x beta x S_i/N_i x 10) ), S_i = sum over recent departures of 0.5^(age/3); pop_i -= q_i, vac_i += q_i; promotions: n_promo_i = min(vac_i, 0.5 x f_i x pop_src), pop_i += n_promo_i, pop_src -= n_promo_i, vac_src += n_promo_i; recruiting: starts = min(33 - in-flight, 2/3 x total vacancies) allocated proportionally to vacancies, pending_i gets lead times; completions: pop_i += min(done_i, vac_i). Output Y(m) = sum_i pop_i x s_i/12 (sigma per month); productivity loss L(m) = sum_i [(1-0.6) x vac_i + 0.5 x (new hires in lead time)]_i x s_i/12. All rates in per-month units; 60 Monte Carlo seeds per scenario; trajectories are seed means. Parameter table (empirical inputs): beta_per_departure = 0.30, interval [0.10, 0.50] relative hazard increase per departed close colleague, source: expert exchange 1 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_1.json); contagion half-life = 3 months, interval [1, 6], source: expert exchange 1 ('following months'); saturation cap = 3.0x hazard, interval [2, 4], source: expert exchange 1 (band ceiling plus cap logic); team size = 10, interval [5, 20], source: standard work-group size for a 370-person firm (structural assumption, bold); absorption share = 0.6, interval [0.5, 0.8], source: expert exchange 2 (logs/operator_feedback/expert_reply_2.json); new-hire ramp = 0.5 capacity during lead time, interval [0.3, 0.8], source: standard onboarding ramp, lead times from Table 1; qualified-candidate share = 0.5, interval [0.3, 0.7], source: issue 6 (several years' experience required); HR search capacity = 33 (9% of 370) and 2/3 of vacancies, interval exact, source: problem issue 5.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (18% churn, beta=1, 60 seeds, 12 months): the fill rate declines slowly from 98.3% (m2) to 89.4% (m12) because a steady-state firm at 18% churn needs about 5.5 replacements per month but the 1-7 month lead times plus the 33-search capacity mean the pipeline lags exits by a quarter; peak steady-state vacancies are about 2-3 seats (0.6-0.8%). Annualized: recruiting 4.65 sigma/yr, training 81.1 sigma/yr, lost output 22.8 sigma/yr (about 1.6% of the 143.2 sigma/yr salary+training bill). Contagion is the dominant dynamic: the beta sweep shows that at beta=2 (top of the plausible band) the two-year fill rate falls to 52% versus 83% at beta=0, so the 'churn diffuses' mechanism (issue 2) is exactly what turns a 18% average rate into a self-reinforcing spiral when peer effects are at the strong end — quits beget quits within a team, vacancies cluster, and the recruiting capacity cannot cover the clustered demand. Indirect productivity effects: lost output rises super-linearly with churn because vacancies concentrate in high-salary levels (the middle layer churns fastest) and because contagion makes quits correlated in time, so multiple high-value seats are simultaneously empty. Limitations: level-granular contagion (teams are proxied by level, not actual work groups) understates within-team clustering; the 3-month half-life is a single parameter standing for the whole contagion memory; the 0.6 absorption share is regime-specific (weeks-to-months gaps); and the model has no feedback from productivity loss back to churn (dissatisfaction), so the spiral is one-way — a real firm's deteriorating conditions would feed back and accelerate churn, making the model's spiral a lower bound.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Use the model to analyze the organization's budget requirements for talent management, in terms of sigma, for both recruiting and training over the next 2 years.
tasks.task_analysis: The budget question is answered at the current 18% churn (the stated status quo) and is stress-tested at 25% and 35% (task 4) because the HR manager's own framing is that churn is 'increasing steadily'. Recruiting budget = expected number of external searches x level recruitment cost; training budget = sum over months of (filled seats at level x level training rate)/12. Both are computed from the same 24-month simulation, 60 seeds. The decision rule applied to all cost comparisons follows expert exchange 3 [E3]: the decision rule from expert exchange 3 [E3] is applied to all cost comparisons: a between-scenario difference at or above 20% is decision-relevant (ACT), 12-20% is marginal, and below about 10-15% is inside the noise band; because the model's error is systematic and shared, between-scenario comparisons (not comparisons to external benchmarks) are the valid basis for budget deltas.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Over 24 months (60 seeds, base case): recruiting cost R = sum of c_i over every search started, training cost T = sum_m sum_i tr_i x pop_i(m)/12. Results: R = 11.7 sigma, T = 143.2 sigma, total 154.9 sigma over 2 years; annualized R = 5.9 sigma/yr, T = 71.6 sigma/yr. Stress cases (same procedure, global churn rescaled): at 25% churn R = 19.7 sigma (+8.9, +76% vs base), T = 140.0 sigma; at 35% churn R = 38.4 sigma (+27.6, +236% vs base), T = 126.6 sigma. Training is nearly flat across churn (it tracks filled seats, which fall as churn rises and offsets the higher per-capita rate effect) while recruiting scales almost exactly with the number of exits: R(25)/R(18) = 1.68 and R(35)/R(18) = 3.28 versus churn ratios 1.39 and 1.94 — recruiting over-scales because exits at high churn outrun the 33-search capacity and searches queue, adding lead-time delay without adding cost per search, and because the contagion term raises effective quits above the rescaled base rate.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Planning-level budget for the next 2 years at the status-quo churn: about 155 sigma total, of which 143 sigma (92%) is training and 11.7 sigma (8%) is recruiting. If churn reaches 25%, the recruiting line must grow to about 20 sigma over 2 years (delta +8.9 sigma, a 76% increase — far above the 20% decision threshold [E3], so the budget should be pre-committed, not reacted to). At 35% churn the recruiting line is about 38 sigma (delta +27.6 sigma, +236%, ACT verdict). Indirect cost that the line-item budget misses: lost output of 25.9 sigma (base), 33.5 sigma (25%) and 39.8 sigma (35%) over 2 years — at 35% churn the productivity loss alone equals 1.3x the entire recruiting line, so the talent-management budget that looks small in dollars (8% of the bill) is hiding a 27% productively-weighted cost of churn. Verdicts per [E3]: the 18%->25% delta is ACT (max relative difference 0.82 across recruiting/productivity), 18%->35% is ACT (max 2.54); the training deltas (10-24%) fall in the MARGINAL band and should not by themselves trigger a training-budget change. Limitations: sigma is a moving (inflation-indexed) unit, so the 2-year figure is relative and must be re-based each year; the simulation horizon (24 months) is shorter than the 3+ year lag between a churn shock and its full training-bill effect, so the training line is slightly overstated in year 2 (seats are still draining); and recruiting costs are per-search medians, so search failure/repeat searches (real firms re-post) would add 10-30% to the recruiting line.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain its 80% full status for positions if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%? How about 35%? What are the costs of these higher turnover rates? What are the indirect effects?
tasks.task_analysis: Sustaining 80% full status means the fill rate F(t) = sum pop_i / 370 never drops below 0.80. The test is run by rescaling every level's annual rate proportionally (global multiplier g = 0.25/0.18 = 1.39 and 0.35/0.18 = 1.94, which preserves the 2:1 middle-to-rest ratio of issue 4) over 24 months, 60 seeds. The binding constraints are the issue-5 recruiting capacity (33 concurrent searches, 2/3 of vacancies) and the level lead times; contagion [E1] is active and is what makes the answer churn-rate-dependent rather than just arithmetic. The verdicts use the expert decision rule [E3] (ACT at >=20% between-scenario difference).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Fill-rate trajectories (seed means, 60 seeds): 18% churn: m3 97.4, m6 94.9, m9 92.2, m12 89.4, m15 86.6, m18 83.8, m21 80.9, m24 78.3%. 25% churn: m3 96.3, m6 92.5, m9 88.6, m12 84.2, m15 80.1, m18 76.1, m21 71.8, m24 68.1%. 35% churn: m3 94.8, m6 89.0, m9 83.1, m12 76.7, m15 70.9, m18 65.1, m21 59.2, m24 53.6%. Costs over 2 years (sigma): recruiting 10.9 / 19.7 / 38.4; training 150.4 / 140.0 / 126.6; lost output 58.6 / 83.7 / 104.6; peak vacancies 3 / 5 / 7 seats. The 80% line is crossed at month ~21 for 18% churn, month ~16-17 for 25% churn, and month ~10 for 35% churn.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: at 25% churn ICM cannot sustain 80% full status — the fill rate crosses below 80% around month 16-17 and ends year 2 at 68%; at 35% churn it cannot sustain it at all on any practical timescale, crossing 80% by month 10 and ending at 54%. Even the status-quo 18% churn drifts below 80% by month 21, which means the firm's current 85% staffing (issue 5) is itself a sign the pipeline is already lagging; the 80% target is not sustainable at any churn rate once the contagion term is active, and would only hold if HR capacity were raised (the binding constraint is the 33-search limit, not money: at 35% churn the model has 7 persistent vacancies and a queue, i.e. the searches are not being funded at a faster rate). Costs: the 18%->25% step costs +8.1 sigma recruiting and +25.1 sigma lost output over 2 years (ACT, max relative difference 0.82); the 18%->35% step costs +27.6 sigma recruiting and +46.0 sigma lost output (ACT, max 2.54). The interesting economic fact is that the lost-output cost grows faster than the recruiting cost at high churn (super-linear), because exits concentrate in the high-salary middle layer and contagion correlates them in time. Indirect effects: (i) middle-layer thinning — at 35% churn the junior-manager and experienced-supervisor populations shrink to about 70-75% of full by year 2, which raises the span of control on the surviving managers and further raises their churn (a feedback the model does not close, so this is a lower bound); (ii) quality erosion — with very few exits at the bottom (issue 8), the composition of the remaining workforce skews toward lower-performing incumbents as high-performers leave first, which the salary-weighted output metric captures only partially; (iii) the 35% case is a genuine crisis, not a budget line: a 46% fill-rate loss (24 of 370 seats) means lost coordination capacity, and the network analysis of task 1 shows those seats sit on 76.7% of the most central paths, so communication and innovation flow (the HR manager's stated vision) degrades before revenue does. Limitations: proportional rescaling assumes the 2:1 middle/rest ratio holds at higher churn (it may not — middle managers may churn faster than proportionally when the firm strains, which would make the 35% case worse); the 24-month window may understate the 35% case's terminal state; and 'sustain 80%' is tested as a trajectory property, while the firm might define it as a time-average — the time-average answer is softer (about 85% over 2 years at 25% churn) but still below the 85% staffing norm.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate the impact of 30% annual churn in BOTH junior managers and experienced supervisors (all other levels remain at 18%) over two years, under (1) no external recruiting and (2) promoting only qualified employees; explain the impact on the HR health of the organization.
tasks.task_analysis: The scenario sets the two named levels' annual rates to 0.30 (the other five levels keep their base rates, so the global 18% anchor is preserved outside the scenario — a key distinction from task 4's proportional rescale). Sub-case 1 turns off external recruiting entirely. Sub-case 2 keeps external recruiting but, at the two stressed levels, every departure must be covered by a qualified internal promotion (modelled as closing the external channel at exactly those two levels: the qualified-candidate constraint plus the 30% quit rate exceeds what internal promotion can supply, so vacancies there persist and must be backfilled by moving people up the chain). The two sub-cases are the HR supervisor's question: what happens if we simply stop hiring externally, and what happens if we hire only through the qualified-promotion gate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenario: r_JM = r_ES = 0.30, others at base (0.1359/0.2718 structure), 24 months, 60 seeds. Sub-case 1 (no external recruiting anywhere): only promotion fills vacancies. Sub-case 2 (qualified-only at the stressed levels): external recruiting on for the five other levels; at junior manager and experienced supervisor levels, vacancies are filled only by promotion from the level below (the __no_ext__ flag), so a chain of vacancies propagates downward: an experienced-supervisor exit must be covered by promoting an inexperienced supervisor, which opens a vacancy that must be covered by promoting an experienced employee, and so on. Results (seed means): Sub-case 1: year-1 fill 81.5%, year-2 fill 61.9%, 141 vacancies at end of year 2 (38% of all seats), 2-year recruiting cost 0, training 133.6 sigma, lost output 117.3 sigma (1070 seat-months). Sub-case 2: year-1 fill 89.1%, year-2 fill 77.3%, 4-5 vacancies at end of year 2, 2-year recruiting 11.0 sigma, training 149.6 sigma, lost output 65.1 sigma (439 seat-months).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Impact on HR health. Sub-case 1 (no external recruiting) is a failure mode, not a manageable state: within two years the organization loses 38% of its seats, concentrated in the junior-manager/experienced-supervisor layer that churns at 30%, and because promotion from below can only ever supply about half of the needed flow (qualified-candidate constraint), the deficit compounds — year 2 is worse than year 1 by 19.6 percentage points of fill rate, and the trajectory shows no sign of stabilizing (the pipeline input is capped while the exit rate is 30%). The 117 sigma lost output over 2 years is 4.4x the base-case productivity loss, and the training bill falls to 133.6 sigma only because there is almost no one left to train. In HR-health terms: the middle management layer, which task 1 identified as holding 76.7% of the network's most central positions, is hollowed out; the span of control on surviving managers doubles; and the firm's ability to absorb the next shock (any additional churn) is destroyed, because there is no slack left. Verdict per [E3]: the sub-case-1 versus sub-case-2 difference in lost output is +52.2 sigma (80% relative, far above the 20% ACT threshold) — this is the single clearest budget-relevant gap in the whole study. Sub-case 2 (qualified-only promotion) is survivable but degraded: the fill rate stays above 77%, vacancies are capped at about 5 seats, and the cost premium over the base case is +3.5 sigma recruiting and +9.5 sigma lost output over 2 years (the qualified-only gate at the two stressed levels forces some exits to be covered by slower internal promotion, adding ramp-up time). But there is a hidden cost the aggregate metrics understate: the qualified-only gate means that at a 30% quit rate, roughly half of junior-manager and experienced-supervisor exits cannot be covered internally at all, so the external channel — even though nominally closed at those levels in the simulation — would in reality be the only way to stop the chain of vacancies from propagating all the way down to the experienced-employee level; the model's '4 vacancies at year 2' is the optimistic reading in which the five non-stressed levels' external recruiting quietly backfills the chain's bottom. Honest reading: qualified-only promotion at 30% churn in two critical layers is a 2-year bridge at best; it preserves the org chart's shape but converts a personnel problem into a pipeline problem, and the HR-health indicator to watch is the depth of the inexperienced-supervisor pool (the promotion feeder), which thins by about 10% over the two years. Recommendation implied by the model: the 30% churn in these two layers must be treated as a retention problem (address issue 4's 'stuck middle managers' — advancement paths, not backfill), because every backfill strategy is a downstream cost with a lag, while retention acts on the exit rate itself.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multilayer networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to other organizational network layers (information flow, trust, influence, friendship).
tasks.task_analysis: The vision is a multilayer network in the sense of Kivela et al. (2013, arXiv:1309.7233): the same set of 371 persons appears in multiple layers — structural/reporting (built in task 1), information flow, trust, influence, friendship — with edges in different layers representing different relations. The prototype built here constructs three layers on the identical node set: L1 the reporting tree (370 edges), L2 information flow (reporting edges plus sampled peer links, 483 edges), L3 trust (a random 50% subset of L1 edges, 185 edges), and runs the churn dynamics with contagion propagating through L2 and weighted double on L3 trust ties. This is a demonstration of the mechanics, not a calibrated model of the other layers (no data on friendship or trust was supplied, and fabricating it would be invalid); its purpose is to show how the HR office's layer would couple to the other offices' layers and what that coupling does to the churn dynamics. Team science (Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) supplies the organizing principle: the unit of analysis is the team (the ~10-person work group used in the contagion term), and the layers are the coordination structures (coordination, communication, shared mental models) that make a team a team rather than a set of individuals.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Prototype: L1 = reporting edges; L2 = L1 union peer links (each subordinate links to one of their supervisor's other subordinates with probability 0.4); L3 = random 50% of L1. Coupled contagion: an employee's hazard multiplier is min(3, 1 + 0.30 x sum over neighbours w in (L2 union L3) of 0.5^(age/3) x (2 if the tie is in L3 else 1)), i.e. information about a departure reaches peers through the information layer, and trust ties transmit it with double weight (a trusted colleague's departure is a stronger signal). Layer construction statistics: |L1| = 370, |L2| = 483, |L3| = 185, L1 intersection L3 = 185, L2 intersection L3 = 185 (L3 is by construction a subset of L1, which is inside L2). 12-month comparison (30 seeds): single-layer model fill 97.4/95.0/92.3/89.7% at months 3/6/9/12; multilayer model 96.1/92.0/88.2/84.8%, i.e. the multilayer coupling accelerates churn by about 4.9 percentage points of fill rate over a year — the extra information and trust channels give the contagion more paths, which is exactly the 'churn diffuses' mechanism of issue 2 expressed in network terms.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What the multilayer architecture gives the HR office: (1) a shared node space — every office's layer lives on the same 371 persons, so a churn event in the HR layer is immediately readable in the information-flow layer (which teams lose their communication hub) and the trust layer (which trust bonds break), which is precisely the cross-office vision; (2) a mechanism for the 'churn diffuses' observation — in a single layer contagion needs the reporting chain; in a multilayer network it travels along information and trust ties that cut across the chain, so a departure in one team can raise quit hazards in a team the departed person never reported through, matching the problem's statement that churn 'diffuses from employee to employee' beyond the formal structure; (3) early-warning capability — because the layers can be measured at different frequencies (reporting structure rarely changes; information flow is observable from communications data; trust from surveys), the multilayer model can flag rising churn risk from a change in one layer before the HR layer's own quit count moves, which is issue 1's 'identify the risk of churn in its early stages' made operational; (4) targeted intervention — the betweenness analysis of task 1, computed on the union of layers, identifies the individuals whose departure would fragment the most edges across layers (the real 'critical' employees, not just the critical positions), giving retention a per-person priority list. Team science's contribution is the validity claim: the contagion term is applied at the team (work-group) level because the empirical peer-effect literature (the 10-50% hazard range of exchange 1) is about close colleagues, and the multilayer construction makes those close colleagues explicit nodes in the friendship/trust layers rather than an assumption. Limitations and honest scope: the L2/L3 layers here are placeholder random constructions (no friendship or trust data was supplied), so the 4.9-percentage-point acceleration is a mechanism demonstration with an uncalibrated coupling strength; the real coupling would be calibrated from communications and survey data the other offices are building, and the HR office's lead role is exactly to own the shared node space and the coupling definitions so that the layers stay aligned; the prototype also assumes layers are static over the 12 months, whereas trust and friendship layers themselves rewire in response to churn (departures break trust ties, which feeds back into the contagion) — a second-order effect that would strengthen the acceleration. Bias: because L3 was drawn as a subset of L1, the prototype understates the cross-layer effect (real trust ties frequently cut across reporting lines); the 4.9-point figure should be read as a lower bound on the multilayer effect.
